'''G. Peter Lepage''' (born 13 April 1952) is a [[Canadian Americans|Canadian American]] [[Theoretical physics|theoretical physicist]] and an [[Academic administration|academic administrator]].<ref name=":0">{{Cite web|url=https://physics.cornell.edu/peter-lepage|title=Peter Lepage {{!}} Department of Physics Cornell Arts & Sciences|last=|first=|date=|website=physics.cornell.edu|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20180613053929/http://physics.cornell.edu/peter-lepage|archive-date=June 13, 2018|url-status=live|access-date=2018-12-04|df=mdy-all}}</ref> He was the [[Harold Tanner]] Dean of the [[Cornell University College of Arts and Sciences|College of Arts and Sciences]] at [[Cornell University]] from 2003 to 2013.<ref name=":0" /><ref name=":1">{{Cite web|url=https://news.cornell.edu/stories/2003/12/g-peter-lepage-appointed-dean-cornell-college-arts-and-sciences|title=G. Peter Lepage appointed dean of Cornell College of Arts and Sciences|last=|first=|date=|website=Cornell Chronicle|language=en|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20180124054737/http://news.cornell.edu/stories/2003/12/g-peter-lepage-appointed-dean-cornell-college-arts-and-sciences|archive-date=January 24, 2018|url-status=live|access-date=2018-12-04|df=mdy-all}}</ref>

== Early life and education ==
Gerard Peter Lepage was born in Canada in 1952. Lepage studied at [[McGill University]] and graduated with a bachelor's degree in honours physics in 1972 and the [[University of Cambridge]] with a master's degree ([[Part III of the Mathematical Tripos|M.A.St]] - [[Part III of the Mathematical Tripos]]) in 1973.<ref name=":0" /> In 1978, he received his [[Doctor of Philosophy|PhD]] in theoretical physics from [[Stanford University]].<ref name=":0" />

== Academic career ==
Lepage was a research associate at the [[SLAC National Accelerator Laboratory|Stanford Linear Accelerator Center]] in 1978. He was a postdoctoral research associate at the Laboratory of Nuclear Studies, Cornell University from 1978 to 1980. In 1980, he joined the physics faculty at Cornell University where he became a professor.<ref name=":0" /> He received [[Academic tenure in North America|academic tenure]] in 1984 after only four years on the university faculty.<ref name=":1" /> From 1999 to 2003, he was the chair of Cornell's physics department. He was appointed the Harold Tanner Dean of the College of Arts and Sciences, serving from 2003 to 2013.

He is a Fellow of the [[American Academy of Arts and Sciences]] and a Fellow of the [[American Physical Society]].<ref name=":0" /> He was previously an [[Sloan Research Fellowship|Alfred P. Sloan Fellow]] (1983–85; 1990) and [[Guggenheim Fellowship|John Simon Guggenheim Fellow]] (1996–97) Since 2012 he has been a member of the National Science Board.<ref name=":2" />

G. Peter Lepage has been a visiting scholar at a number of institutions: the [[Institute for Advanced Study|Institute for Advanced Study, Princeton]]; [[Faculty of Mathematics, University of Cambridge|Department of Applied Mathematics and Theoretical Physics, Cambridge]]; the University of California Institute of Theoretical Physics, Santa Barbara, the Fermi National Accelerator Center near [[Chicago]], and the Institute for Nuclear Theory, [[Seattle]].<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.ias.edu/scholars/g-peter-lepage|title=G. Peter Lepage|last=|first=|date=|website=Institute for Advanced Study|language=en|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20171203042313/https://www.ias.edu/scholars/g-peter-lepage|archive-date=December 3, 2017|url-status=live|access-date=2018-12-04|df=mdy-all}}</ref>

He was on the editorial board of [[Physical Review|Physical Review D]] and [[Physical Review Letters]] and received the Outstanding Referee Award from the APS in 2009.<ref name=":2" /> He has served on the scientific program committees for the Stanford Linear Accelerator Center, the DOE-[[National Science Foundation|NSF]] National Computational Infrastructure for Lattice Gauge Theory, the NSF's Institute for Nuclear Theory in Seattle, the International Particle Data Group, and the NSF's Institute for Theoretical Physics in [[Santa Barbara, California|Santa Barbara]].<ref name=":2" />

He was the co-chair of the working group for the [[Barack Obama|President Obama]]’s [[United States President's Council of Advisors on Science and Technology|Council of Advisors on Science and Technology]] (PCAST) on [[Science, technology, engineering, and mathematics|STEM]] teaching at colleges and universities, which in 2012 produced the acclaimed report, ''“Engage to Excel: Producing One Million Additional College Graduates with Degrees in Science, Technology, Engineering, and Mathematics.”''<ref name=":2">
{{Cite web|url=https://www.nsf.gov/nsb/members/current_members/Lepage.jsp|title=National Science Board-Current Members|last=|first=|date=|website=|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20170604012517/https://nsf.gov/nsb/members/current_members/lepage.jsp|archive-date=June 4, 2017|url-status=dead|access-date=|df=mdy-all}}
</ref> He has served on the technical advisory committee for the [[Association of American Universities]]’ Undergraduate STEM Education Initiative, and is vice chair of the [[National Science Board]]’s Committee on Education and Human Resources.<ref name=":2" />

He is also involved in innovations in [[pedagogy]], especially physics education at all levels.<ref name=":2" /> He spearheads the Active Learning Initiative (ALI) in Cornell's college of arts and sciences, a five-year pilot project, funded by 1987 alumni, Alex and Laura Hanson, used to enhance strategies for interactive classroom learning using emerging technologies.<ref name=":4">{{Cite web|url=https://news.cornell.edu/stories/2015/10/peter-lepage-lead-education-innovation-arts-and-sciences|title=Peter Lepage to lead education, innovation at Arts and Sciences|last=|first=|date=|website=Cornell Chronicle|language=en|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20180411140950/http://news.cornell.edu/stories/2015/10/peter-lepage-lead-education-innovation-arts-and-sciences|archive-date=April 11, 2018|url-status=live|access-date=2018-12-04|df=mdy-all}}</ref>

=== Research ===
In the late 1970s and early 1980s, he was known for his research with [[Stanley Brodsky]] on [[quantum chromodynamics]] (QCD) and perturbation theory of scattering processes,<ref name=":0" /> His research focus examines high precision calculations, adapted to [[renormalization]] techniques and effective field theory.<ref name=":2" /><ref>{{cite arXiv|last=Lepage|first=G. Peter|date=2005-06-30|title=What is Renormalization?|eprint=hep-ph/0506330|df=mdy-all}}</ref> This method is then applied to the fields of QCD in [[atomic physics]], computational [[quantum field theory]], [[condensed matter physics]], [[nuclear physics]] (little body problem), systems of heavy [[quark]]s and exclusive scattering processes with high momentum transfer.<ref name=":0" />

His research also covers [[Supercomputer|high-performance computing]] (HPC) or large scale numerical simulations of non-perturbative lattice QCD, leading in part to a range of calculations at different observation sizes – [[quark]]s, [[gluon]]s and [[hadron]] masses, coupling constants and mixing angles in the [[Standard Model]], magnetic moment of muons and allowed to determine the QCD contributions for precision testing of the Standard Model (distinguishable from possible contributions of new physics beyond the standard model).<ref name=":0" /> These particles describe the inner structure of protons, neutrons and other sub-nuclear particles. His research resulted in the [[VEGAS algorithm]] for adaptive method for reducing error in [[Monte Carlo method|Monte Carlo simulations]] in interaction physics by using a known or approximate probability distribution function.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://github.com/gplepage|title=gplepage - Overview|last=|first=|date=|website=GitHub|language=en|access-date=2018-12-04}}</ref>

In 2016, Lepage received the [[Sakurai Prize|J. J. Sakurai Prize]] from the American Physical Society for ''“innovative applications of quantum field theory in elementary particle physics, in particular for the justification of the theory of exclusive processes, the development of nonrelativistic effective field theories and the determination of parameters of the standard model with lattice theories.”''<ref name=":3">{{Cite web|last=|first=|date=|title=2016 J. J. Sakurai Award Recipient|url=https://www.aps.org/programs/honors/prizes/sakurai.cfm|url-status=live|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210426181832/https://www.aps.org/programs/honors/prizes/sakurai.cfm|archive-date=April 26, 2021|access-date=2021-12-17|website=www.aps.org|language=en|df=mdy-all}}</ref>

He has authored more than 250 scientific publications.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.researchgate.net/scientific-contributions/54668568_G_Peter_Lepage|title=G. Peter Lepage's research works {{!}} Cornell University, Ithaca (CU) and other places|last=|first=|date=|website=ResearchGate|language=en|access-date=2018-12-04}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web|url=https://scholar.google.com/citations?user=Oig8PGwAAAAJ&hl=en|title=G. Peter Lepage - Google Scholar Citations|website=scholar.google.com|access-date=2018-12-04}}</ref> In 2002, together with fellow academics, [[Carolyn Martin|Carolyn (Biddy) Martin]] and [[Mohsen Mostafavi]], he co-edited a book on the future and relevance of the humanities, ''“Do the Humanities Have to Be Useful?”''<ref>{{Cite book|title=Do the Humanities Have to Be Useful?|df=mdy-all|isbn = 978-0978551407|last1 = Peter Lepage|first1 = G.|last2=Martin|first2=Biddy|last3=Mostafavi|first3=Mohsen|year=2006|publisher=Cornell University }}</ref>

== Personal life ==
G. Peter Lepage is married to Deborah O'Connor and they have three sons: Michael, Daniel and Matthew.<ref name=":1" /> O'Connor studied [[pharmacology]] at Stanford, worked in biochemistry at Cornell and served on the [[Ithaca City School District]] Board of Education.<ref name=":1" />
